skills.title: Data Tables
skills.summary: A data table organizes measurements in labelled rows and columns, with the independent variable usually in the first column and the dependent variable beside it. Headings must name the quantity and its unit so the data can be read without ambiguity.
objectives: Read a value from a data table.
Explain what belongs in table headings.
Organize measurements into a table.

skills.title: Categorical and Numerical Data
skills.summary: Categorical data sorts observations into named groups such as color or species, while numerical data records measured or counted amounts. The type of data determines which graph is appropriate.
objectives: Classify data as categorical or numerical.
Give examples of each type.
Explain how data type affects graph choice.

skills.title: Reading Axes
skills.summary: Every graph axis has a label naming the quantity, a unit, and a scale of evenly spaced intervals. Reading a graph correctly means checking what each axis represents and how much each division is worth before interpreting any point.
objectives: Identify what each axis of a graph represents.
Determine the value of one scale division.
Read a point's value from labelled axes.

skills.title: Bar Graphs
skills.summary: A bar graph compares categorical data using bars whose heights show the value for each category. The bars are separated because the categories are distinct groups rather than a continuous scale.
objectives: Read a value from a bar graph.
Explain when a bar graph is the right choice.
Compare categories using bar heights.

skills.title: Line Graphs
skills.summary: A line graph shows how a numerical quantity changes across a continuous scale such as time, with points joined to reveal the pattern of change. Line graphs suit continuous data, unlike bar graphs which compare categories.
objectives: Read a value from a line graph.
Explain when a line graph is appropriate.
Describe what a rising or falling line means.

skills.title: Scatter Plots
skills.summary: A scatter plot shows paired measurements of two numerical variables as separate points, revealing whether they are related. Points are not joined, because the aim is to show the overall pattern rather than a sequence.
objectives: Explain what a scatter plot displays.
Describe a positive, negative, or absent relationship.
Explain why scatter points are not joined.

skills.title: Trends
skills.summary: A trend is the overall direction of a data set: increasing, decreasing, or staying roughly constant. Describing a trend means summarizing the general pattern rather than listing every individual value.
objectives: Describe the trend in a data set.
Distinguish a trend from an individual fluctuation.
Use a trend to make a prediction.

skills.title: Outliers
skills.summary: An outlier is a value that lies far away from the rest of the data. Outliers may come from measurement or recording mistakes, or may be genuine and important, so they are investigated rather than silently deleted.
objectives: Identify an outlier in a data set.
Give possible causes of an outlier.
Explain how outliers should be handled.

skills.title: Proportional Relationships in Data
skills.summary: Two quantities in data are proportional when their ratio stays constant, so doubling one doubles the other. On a graph a proportional relationship appears as a straight line passing through the origin.
objectives: Decide from data whether two quantities are proportional.
Recognize a proportional relationship on a graph.
Use a constant ratio to predict a value.

skills.title: Drawing Conclusions from Data
skills.summary: A conclusion states what the data shows about the original question, referring to the evidence and saying whether it supports the hypothesis. A sound conclusion stays within what the data can show and acknowledges its limitations.
objectives: Write a conclusion that refers to the evidence.
Judge whether data supports a hypothesis.
Recognize a conclusion that goes beyond the data.

components.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to read and construct a clear data table.
Recall that an observation is information gathered with the senses or instruments. Tables are how those observations get organized.

A table is a grid that keeps measurements tidy. Reading down the first column tells you what was changed; reading across a row tells you what was measured for that value. Labelled headings mean anyone can interpret it later.

A data table arranges values in rows and columns with headings that state the quantity and its unit, such as 'Time (s)'. The independent variable is conventionally placed in the first column and the dependent variable in the next.
Consider this table. Time (s): 0, 1, 2, 3. Distance (m): 0, 5, 10, 15. Each row pairs a time with the distance measured at that time.
Using the table above, what distance corresponds to a time of 2 s? Find the row where Time is 2 and read across: the distance is 10 m.
In the same table, what is the distance at time 3 s? Reading across that row gives 15 m.
A common mistake is omitting units from headings, which makes a number meaningless: '5' could be 5 metres or 5 kilometres.
Data tables organize measurements in labelled rows and columns, with units in the headings and the independent variable first.
Why must a table heading include the unit as well as the quantity?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to classify data as categorical or numerical and connect the type to graph choice.
Recall that data tables organize measurements with labelled headings.

Recording the color of each car in a car park gives you labels: red, blue, white. Recording each car's length gives you numbers. Labels group things; numbers measure them, and you can do arithmetic only with the numbers.

Categorical data places observations into named categories (eye color, material, species). Numerical data consists of counts or measurements (length, mass, time, temperature) on which arithmetic is meaningful. Categorical data is usually shown with bar graphs; numerical data that changes continuously suits line graphs.
Is 'favorite fruit' categorical or numerical? The values are names such as apple or banana, which are categories, so it is categorical data.
Is the height of a plant in centimeters categorical or numerical? It is a measurement, so it is numerical.
A common mistake is treating numbered labels as numerical data. A jersey number identifies a player and is really a category, even though it looks like a number.
Categorical data sorts into named groups; numerical data records counts or measurements. The distinction determines which graph type suits the data.
How can you tell numerical data from categorical data that happens to use numbers?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to interpret graph axes, scales, and the value of a division.
Recall the coordinate plane, where the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis meet at the origin.

Before reading any graph, look at its edges. The labels tell you what is being plotted and the numbers tell you how much each gridline is worth. If five divisions cover 10 units, each division is 2 units, and misreading that turns every value you take off the graph into a wrong number.

An axis has a label (the quantity), a unit, and a scale of equal intervals. The independent variable is conventionally on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis. The value of one division equals the range covered divided by the number of divisions.
An axis runs from 0 to 10 with 5 equal divisions. Each division is worth 10 divided by 5 = 2 units.
An axis runs from 0 to 20 with 4 equal divisions. Each division is worth 20 divided by 4 = 5 units.
A common mistake is assuming every gridline equals one unit. Always compute the division value from the labelled numbers before reading points.
Axes carry a label, a unit, and an evenly spaced scale. Work out the value of one division first, then read points; the independent variable normally goes on the x-axis.
How do you work out how much one division on an axis is worth?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to read and choose bar graphs appropriately.
Recall that categorical data sorts into named groups, and that axes carry labels, units, and scales.

Counting how many students prefer each of four fruits, you draw one bar per fruit. The taller the bar, the more students. Because apples and bananas are separate groups rather than points on a scale, the bars stand apart.

A bar graph displays categorical data as bars whose lengths are proportional to their values. Categories go along one axis and the measured value along the other; bars are drawn separated to show that the categories are discrete.
Consider a bar graph of pets owned. Dogs: 8, Cats: 6, Fish: 3, Birds: 2. Each bar's height gives the count for that category.
Using that graph, which pet is most common? The tallest bar is dogs at 8, so dogs are most common.
How many more dogs than fish are there? 8 - 3 = 5 more.
A common mistake is joining the tops of bars with a line. Categories are not a continuous scale, so a connecting line has no meaning.
Bar graphs compare distinct categories using bar heights, with bars separated because the categories are discrete.
Why are the bars on a bar graph drawn separated rather than touching?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to read line graphs and choose them appropriately.
Recall reading axes: check the label, unit, and value of each division before taking readings.

Recording a cooling drink's temperature every minute and joining the points shows the story of the cooling: steep at first, then flattening. Joining makes sense because temperature exists at every instant between your readings.

A line graph plots points for a numerical dependent variable against a continuous independent variable, usually time, and joins them. Joining is valid only when values exist between the plotted points. A rising line shows increase, a falling line decrease, and a flat line no change.
Consider a line graph of temperature over time. Time (min): 0, 1, 2, 3. Temperature (degrees C): 90, 80, 72, 66. The line falls steeply then more gently.
Using that graph, what is the temperature at 2 minutes? Reading the point at time 2 gives 72 degrees Celsius.
Between 0 and 1 minute the temperature falls from 90 to 80, a drop of 10 degrees.
A common mistake is using a line graph for categories. Joining points implies values in between, which is meaningless for separate categories.
Line graphs show change across a continuous scale, with joined points revealing the pattern. Rising means increasing, falling means decreasing, flat means unchanged.
When is it valid to join plotted points with a line?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to interpret scatter plots and describe the relationship they show.
Recall line graphs, which join points to show change over a continuous scale, and axis reading.

Measuring the height and arm span of thirty people and plotting each person as one dot, you see a cloud of dots sloping upward: taller people tend to have longer arm spans. No line is drawn because each dot is a separate individual, not a step in a sequence.

A scatter plot displays paired values of two numerical variables as individual points. An upward pattern indicates a positive relationship, a downward pattern a negative relationship, and a shapeless cloud indicates no relationship. Points are not joined because they are independent observations.
In a scatter plot of study time against test score, the dots rise from left to right. This is a positive relationship: more study time is associated with higher scores.
If dots fall from left to right, more of the first variable goes with less of the second: a negative relationship.
A common mistake is concluding that one variable causes the other. A scatter plot shows association only; a controlled experiment is needed to establish cause.
Scatter plots show paired numerical measurements as unjoined points, revealing positive, negative, or no relationship. Association is not proof of cause.
Why are the points on a scatter plot not joined by a line?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe trends and use them to make predictions.
Recall reading line graphs, where a rising line shows increase and a falling line shows decrease.

Plant heights of 2, 5, 7, 10, and 12 cm over five weeks wobble slightly from week to week, but the story is simple: the plant is getting taller. That overall direction is the trend, and small week-to-week variations do not change it.

A trend is the general direction of change in a data set: increasing, decreasing, or approximately constant. Trends are described from the overall pattern, not from single points, and can be used to predict values beyond the measured range with caution.
Heights over five weeks are 2, 5, 7, 10, 12 cm. Each week the value is larger, so the trend is increasing, at roughly 2 to 3 cm per week.
Temperatures of 20, 18, 15, 13 degrees over four hours show a decreasing trend.
A common mistake is calling a single unusual value a change in trend. One dip in an otherwise rising set is a fluctuation, not a reversal.
A trend is the overall direction of a data set. Describe it from the whole pattern, ignore single fluctuations, and use it for cautious predictions.
How do you tell a genuine trend from a one-off fluctuation?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to spot outliers and decide how to handle them properly.
Recall that trends describe the general pattern, and that repeated trials expose random variation.

Among the readings 12, 13, 12, 47, and 13, the value 47 stands out sharply. It might be a slipped decimal point or a misread scale, or it might be a real and interesting event. Either way it deserves a second look, not silent deletion.

An outlier is a data value that differs markedly from the others in a set. Possible causes include measurement error, recording error, equipment fault, or a genuine unusual event. Good practice is to investigate the outlier, repeat the measurement if possible, and report any exclusion with its reason.
In the set 12, 13, 12, 47, 13, the outlier is 47 because every other value clusters near 12 or 13.
In the set 100, 102, 5, 101, the outlier is 5, far below the cluster near 100.
A common mistake is deleting any inconvenient value. Removing data without investigation and without reporting it is poor practice and can hide a real discovery.
An outlier lies far from the rest of the data. Investigate its cause, repeat the measurement where possible, and report any exclusion openly.
Why should an outlier be investigated rather than simply deleted?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to recognize proportional relationships in data and use them to predict.
Recall direct proportionality, where y = k times x, and that its graph is a straight line through the origin.

If 1 kg of a substance has a volume of 2 litres, and 2 kg has 4 litres, and 3 kg has 6 litres, the ratio of volume to mass is always 2. Doubling the mass doubles the volume, and a graph of the pairs would be a straight line running through the origin.

Two quantities are proportional when their ratio is constant, so y divided by x equals the same constant k for every pair. The graph is a straight line through the origin. If the line is straight but does not pass through the origin, the relationship is linear but not proportional.
Consider the pairs Mass (kg): 1, 2, 3 and Volume (L): 2, 4, 6. Each volume divided by its mass equals 2, so the points lie on a straight line through the origin.
Are these proportional? Mass 1, 2, 3 kg with volume 2, 4, 6 L. Compute the ratios: 2/1 = 2, 4/2 = 2, 6/3 = 2. The ratio is constant, so yes, they are proportional with constant 2.
Using that constant, what volume corresponds to 5 kg? Multiply: 5 times 2 = 10 L.
A common mistake is calling any straight line proportional. A line that crosses the y-axis above zero has a starting value, so the ratio is not constant and the relationship is not proportional.
Proportional quantities have a constant ratio and graph as a straight line through the origin. A straight line missing the origin is linear but not proportional.
What two features show that a graphed relationship is proportional?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to draw sound conclusions that are supported by data and to spot overreaching ones.
Recall that evidence supports or challenges an idea, and that a trend is the overall direction of the data.

After growing plants in three light levels, a good conclusion says what happened and points at the numbers: plants in bright light grew tallest, averaging 15 cm against 6 cm in dim light. A weak conclusion just says 'light is good for plants', which the numbers never quite showed.

A conclusion answers the investigation's question by stating what the data shows, citing specific evidence, and saying whether the hypothesis is supported. It must not claim more than the data can show, and it should note limitations such as small sample size or uncontrolled factors.

Data: plants under bright light averaged 15 cm, dim light 6 cm, controlled otherwise. Conclusion: the data supports the hypothesis that more light increases growth, since bright-light plants grew about 9 cm taller on average.
If the two groups had grown equally, the conclusion would be that the data does not support the hypothesis, and light showed no measurable effect in this range.

A common mistake is claiming a hypothesis is 'proved'. Data can support or fail to support a hypothesis, but a single experiment does not prove it, and conclusions should not extend beyond the conditions tested.
A conclusion states what the data shows, cites the evidence, judges support for the hypothesis, and stays within the limits of what was measured.
What three things should a good conclusion contain?

answer_spec.correct_answer: so distances along the axis represent equal changes in value

options: so distances along the axis represent equal changes in value
so the graph fits the page

hints.text: Multiply divisions by the division value.

answer_spec.correct_answer: categorical data

questions.explanation: The difference is 8 - 3 = 5.

because the bars are different heights

the line is the wrong color
lines are never allowed on graphs
it makes the graph too tall

questions.prompt: What does a scatter plot display?
